Great questions — answered inline below and attached a small spreadsheet with worked examples (unit-econ-calc.xlsx).

Short answers:
- Characters -> tokens: heuristic we use is ~4 characters per token (English, mixed-case, punctuation). That makes 200M characters ≈ 50M tokens. This is a heuristic; tight prompts or lots of punctuation can change the ratio.
- Cached prompts: when a prompt prefix is eligible for cache and a request hits that cache, Redwood reduces billed input tokens to only the non-cached portion. In other words, a cache hit reduces billed tokens (not just latency). However cached state that reduces generation can depend on how your prompt templates are structured (prefix vs dynamic fields).
- System messages: yes, system messages are treated as input tokens and are billed when sent with a request. If you add server-side persistent instructions that are not sent per request (i.e., applied at runtime without counting toward the request payload), they would not be billed; most customers send system messages as part of the request and therefore count them.
- Requests vs billing: request counts (requests/day, QPS) are primarily used for rate limiting and capacity planning — they don't directly determine billed units except insofar as each request carries input + output tokens.

Example (from the spreadsheet):
- 200M characters ≈ 50M tokens/month.
- Typical prompt (user + system + few-shot example) = 200 tokens input + 400 tokens generated -> 600 tokens billed per request.
- At 150k requests/day x 30 days = 4.5M requests/month; if each were 600 tokens, that would be 2.7B tokens/month (so make sure request distribution and prompt sizes are accounted for — many customers have small fractions of requests that generate large outputs).

Unit-econ note: your $500/1M target is on the aggressive side for hosted public models at large generation volumes. After caching and prompt optimization, many customers see effective blended rates in the $300–$700/1M range depending on model, quantization, and committed discounts. In the attached spreadsheet I included three scenarios (baseline, caching optimized, committed discounted).

Hi Alex — Rishi here (copies of Marissa’s notes and the spreadsheet are great). Quick pragmatic breakdown and recommended next steps.

1) Three quick scenarios (rounded):
- Baseline (no cache, current prompts): 50M tokens/month (from 200M chars) * blended $0.0005/token = $25k/month -> $500/1M tokens.
- Optimized caching (cache ~40% of prefix tokens): effective tokens billed ~30M/month -> with negotiated hosted discount $0.0004/token -> $12k/month -> ~$400/1M tokens effective.
- Committed / Dedicated: with reserved capacity/commit we can get blended unit economics down to ~$0.00025–0.00035/token -> $250–$350/1M tokens depending on term and QPS guarantees.

Notes: these numbers assume an average generation of ~400 tokens for responses on the subset of requests that generate long outputs; a majority of your requests may be much smaller. The spreadsheet has a row-level calc you can paste your exact averages into.

2) Operational ask: to size a pilot I recommend:
- 2-week pilot that mirrors your peak traffic windows (we usually ask for a parity run with a subset of real traffic or a synthetic replay at 25–50% scale).
- Pilot target: 150k requests/day with expected 10M tokens/day target for production warm-up.

3) Commercial options:
- Short pilot (hosted) + consumption billing (fastest).
- 3–6 month committed (discounted) with an upfront minimum (recommended if you value predictable unit economics).
- Dedicated (reserved) for strict latency / isolation — requires a procurement cycle but materially lowers $/1M tokens at scale.

I’ve attached a short mutual action plan that maps stakeholders and timing (mutual-action-plan.docx). Also added the HubSpot link to the ACME opportunity for your procurement team to reference.
